h1: Storing bottled homebrew in Indian heat
title: Storing Bottled Homebrew in Indian Heat | Craft Beer School
desc: How heat affects bottled homebrew, where to store it in an Indian home and how to condition then keep beer cool so it tastes fresh.
teaser: Indian summers are hard on beer. A few simple storage habits keep your homebrew tasting the way it did on day one.
standfirst: Homebrew does two things after bottling: it conditions, then it ages. Heat speeds up both. In much of India that means beer can go from fresh to stale within weeks. Here is how to store bottles so the heat works for you during conditioning and not against you afterwards.
sections: Heat is the main enemy of bottled beer

Beer staling is a set of slow chemical reactions. Oxygen reacts with malt and hop compounds to make flavours of cardboard, honey, sherry and dried fruit. Hop aroma fades. Like most chemical reactions, these run faster as temperature rises. A common rule of thumb in brewing is that staling roughly doubles in speed for every 10 °C rise in storage temperature.

Apply that to an Indian flat. A beer that would stay fresh for three months at 10 °C might taste tired in a month at 30 °C. On a summer afternoon a closed room in Delhi or Nagpur can pass 35 °C. Store beer there and you are ageing it fast.

Bottle conditioning needs warmth. The yeast must ferment the priming sugar to carbonate the beer. Most ale yeasts do that well at 20 to 24 °C in about two weeks. Indian room temperatures above that range will carbonate bottles faster, often in seven to ten days. The yeast may make a few more fruity esters, but at this stage the risk is low.

The mistake is leaving the bottles warm once they are carbonated. After two weeks, open one bottle to check. If the carbonation is right and the beer is reasonably clear, move the batch somewhere cool. Warm storage beyond that point only ages the beer.
Where to store bottles in an Indian home

• A fridge is best. At 3 to 5 °C, beer stays fresh for months. A spare second-hand single door fridge is the most useful upgrade a serious homebrewer in India can make.
  • The coolest room comes next. An inner room with no outside walls, or the floor of a cupboard on the north side of the home, stays cooler than the rest. A cheap thermometer helps you find it.
  • Avoid the kitchen and the loft. Kitchens run hot from cooking. Lofts and spaces near a roof can be the hottest spots in the house.
  • Keep them dark. Light, especially sunlight, reacts with hop compounds to create a skunky smell called lightstruck. Brown glass protects beer far better than green or clear. A closed carton or crate keeps light out completely.

Our guide to brewing in a small Indian apartment has more space-saving ideas.

Keep bottle-conditioned beer upright. The yeast settles in a neat layer at the bottom, which makes pouring clean easier. Bottles stored on their side leave a yeast streak along the length of the glass that clouds the pour. Upright storage also keeps beer off the underside of the crown cap, where liners can taint it over long periods.
Brew for your climate and drink it fresh

Some styles age well and some do not. Hoppy pale ales and IPAs are best within four to six weeks, whatever the storage. Malty, darker and stronger beers hold up longer. In a hot climate, brew batches you will finish within a couple of months. Brew hoppy beers when you can drink them quickly.

Smaller batches help. A 10 litre batch is easier to keep cool than a 20 litre one and is finished before it fades. If you keg, a keg in a fridge is the best storage of all because the beer never leaves the cold. Our guide to kegging homebrew explains the switch.

Scheduled outages are a reality in many Indian cities and towns. A fridge full of beer stays cold for several hours if the door stays shut. Avoid opening it during the outage. A few frozen water bottles in the fridge add thermal mass and help it ride out a longer cut.

Storage is the step most brewers think about last, yet it decides what the beer tastes like when you finally share it. Understanding staling chemistry well enough to plan around it is part of brewing properly. It is not something you can pick up from one recipe.

Your first step: put a cheap digital thermometer in the place you currently store your bottles. Check it at 3 PM on a hot day. If it reads above 28 °C, find a cooler spot this week.
faqs: How long does bottle conditioning take in Indian heat?
Often seven to ten days at typical Indian room temperatures, compared with about two weeks at 20 to 24 °C. Check one bottle before moving the batch somewhere cool.
Can I store homebrew at room temperature?
For a few weeks, yes. Beer stored warm stales much faster, so move bottles to a fridge or the coolest room once they are carbonated.
Why does my homebrew smell skunky?
Light reacting with hop compounds causes that lightstruck smell. Store bottles in the dark, ideally in brown glass.
